We have used “Boolean logic” and the search string “election OR democracy OR vote OR ballot AND violence OR conflict” with a total result of 2.8 million sources.
After narrowing the search to the titles and abstracts in each database, we identified 183 books and articles, which we analyzed with the Mendeley Desktop computer software.
In the second level, we read the abstracts and added the search term “cause” and its synonyms, resulting in 93 articles, reports, or books.

Admittedly, this database-driven search strategy has limitations since it concentrated mainly on peer-reviewed articles while also generating a bibliography of additional books, monographs, and reports, as well as expert recommendations and other essential sources not included in the database queries, which also resulted in major differences when the search string was changed.
Given these limitations, we have used expert opinion for the final selection of sources to insure an accurate picture of the field's state.
Socioeconomic characteristics.
These causes are worth a closer summary, along with selected subcategories that shed further light on them.
Ethnocommunal fragmentation: Some studies found that ethnoreligious grievances have caused election violence, which was diffused by strong social networks.
In Nigeria, for example, violence followed elections after two decades in a “third wave of democratization” due to the polarization aggravated by national ethnoreligious divisions.

Local social networks nurtured by ethnoreligious grievances (Angerbrandt, 2018) spread violence resulting in an election that was a bitter contest with struggles for power by the factional elite groups representing ethnoreligious and regional interests (Angerbrandt, 2018).
If ethnopolitical groups are excluded from power, and significant economic inequalities exist, it will likely provoke violence.
In Sub-Saharan Africa, widespread electoral violence by both government and opposition actors is caused by ethnopolitical exclusion (Fjelde and Höglund, 2016).
In Kenya, ethnopolitical cleavages impact how political parties mobilize their voters, which correlates with electoral violence (Gutiérrez-Romero, 2014).
The 2007 Kenyan general election resulted in the worst ethnic conflict in the country's history.
In Indonesia, postelection violence tends to occur where there is prior experience of ethnocommunal violence.
Ethnic discrimination sometimes triggers violence (Harish and Toha, 2017).
In parts of the Philippines, election violence is caused by “Muslim separatism” and Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) (Linantud, 1998).

In Serbia, electoral violence almost always happens when the elections are accompanied by low standards of democracy (authoritarian rule) combined with limited space for a competitive race and ethnocultural conflict (Mochtak, 2016).
In Russia, the country's ethnic republic and Muslim region, home to much of Russia's minority population, has experienced more electoral fraud and manipulation (Moser and White, 2016).
According to Smith (2009), Kenya and Ethiopia are the epicenters for political and electoral violence due to the electoral contest.
Nevertheless, Kenya experienced more widespread and deadly interethnic violence than Ethiopia due to this contest (Smith, 2009).
Similarly, in another paper by Wanyama and Elklit (2018), Kenya's clientelist politics has turned the Kenyan political parties into ethnoregional organizations.
For this ethnoregionalization, the elections have witnessed intraparty violence during the primaries for selecting parliamentary and civic seat candidates (Wanyama and Elklit, 2018).
Now it is clear that the connection between election violence, communality, and ethnicity is pretty eminent.
Competition: Competition in politics for winning an election is one of the reasons that election violence takes place.
In this section, we will show how competitive politics, electoral fraud, and efforts to reduce competition in the election lead to electoral violence.
Competitive politics/elections: A growing number of studies discuss how competitive politics are causing election violence in Africa and in general.
However, most of the scholars are focusing more on high-intensity violence.
In Ghana, the political parties recruit party foot soldiers using state resources.
These foot soldiers or youth activists are used for committing low-intensity violence to win elections and maintain control over the state resources (Bob-Milliar, 2014).

On a similar note, a weaker challenger in a political contest will be desperate to use more violent preelection competition against the incumbent; however, the incumbent will try to defend their position by using violence.
There is evidence that the strong challenger party will resort to rigging a vote if the competition is close.
The incumbent candidate is expected to rig the election, eventually leading to electoral violence (Gutiérrez-Romero, 2014).
Due to the electoral competition, the Russian authoritarian rulers distribute patronage resources and policy influence on the lower-level politicians.
In return, they show their loyalty to the incumbents by managing elections in favor of them.
And running these patronage networks can sometimes be violent.
In Ukraine, electoral campaigns are influenced by business sectors, and in the local business sector, influential candidates are “Boss” candidates.
It also shows that a higher level of competition among the candidates can lead to voter manipulation, vote buying, and electoral violence (Herron and Sjoberg, 2016).
In another article by Hickman (2011), postelection violence is associated with the competition for land associated with Kenya's population density.
On the other hand, in Zimbabwe, electoral competition between the opposition candidate and incumbent is responsible for the postelection violence.
Postelection violence has a positive relationship with electoral competition (Hickman, 2011).
Violence and intimidation deter potential voters from participating in the election.
In Sri Lankan elections, the opposition candidates have successfully used this strategy; however, the strategy did not affect the national election's polling outcome.
The candidates competing in parliamentary elections in Sri Lanka need to campaign in a large geographical area.
This is why, the candidates depend on the influential local people at the village level, and this opportunity for the campaign with the candidate can even escalate violence (Höglund, 2009).
The stakes of electoral competition are too high for the incumbent in a system where executive and legislative powers are elected.
Because the opposition wins, they use violence to take advantage of limited openings.
In the Philippines, as argued by Linantud (1998), one of the major reasons for pre-1986 violence in elections is “a confrontational political subculture” (Linantud, 1998).
An electoral competition's negative dynamics sometimes include election violence used to affect an electoral process.
A strong bipolar political competition has created two separate political “tribes” in a homogenous society.

The competition becomes so violent that each party formulate goal-oriented and attacking strategies to win elections by employing political cadres to occupy vote centers and/or prevent vote rigging by the opposing party.

In Nigeria, the risks of violence due to the political competition in this country are so high that electioneering is seen as the equivalent of war and may lead to violence both between and within parties, usually occur before the polling day rather than during and after elections (Reeder and Seeberg, 2018).
Salehyan and Linebarger (2015) state that elections are naturally conflictual since the rival parties will compete for power (Salehyan and Linebarger, 2015).
When the local level or national competition between rival parties is low, however, politics becomes a matter of intraparty violence around nominations.
Intraparty violence severely hampers political parties' institutionalization and their ability to improve their capacity to cope with the tickets' stiff competition (Wanyama and Elklit, 2018).
Election fraud: Pressed by many scholars, electoral fraud is essential for internal conflicts (Crost et al., 2013).

In a study in 2007, the Philippines mayoral elections election fraud could help the incumbents the tightly contested elections, which has caused postelection violence and causalities (Crost et al., 2013).
On the other hand, if the electoral observers reported fraud in the election, then the election's outcome receives the opposition party's attention and society.
Then, it increases the potential for subsequent violence (Daxecker, 2012).
People believe that the election had been rigged to trigger an outbreak of electoral violence (Dercon and Gutiérrez-Romero, 2012).
On the other hand, if the incumbents see if they have electoral support in any particular area, then they (their party) will try to use bribery or ballot fraud.
And the study finally confirms that vote buying (fraud) instigates violence in the election (Daxecker, 2012).
Election fraud does not require direct voter contact; instead, it depends on election officials' small networks.
These networks are most valued in places where opposition clutches are active, but in competitive areas where voter pressure is more common, election fraud can trigger violence.
Nevertheless, the 2007 Kenya election shows an inverse relationship between electoral violence and electoral fraud.
In that particular election, the data indicate that election violence decreases when election fraud increases (Hickman, 2011).
Electoral fraud is a clandestine effort to shape election results.
Fraud is procedural violations of electoral law to the outright use of violence against voters.

If allegations of election fraud, whether confirmed or not, can lead to election violence, unproven perception of fraud can be as destructive as the actual fraud toward the electoral process due to violence.

Not necessarily election during and after the civil wars is more violent than the polls in nondemocratic settings, very competitive elections, and especially those marred by electoral fraud (Salehyan and Linebarger, 2015).
Reduce competition: Politicians to reduce their competitiveness in the elections foment violence in the elections to increase their chances of winning.
By killing the politicians who are competing in the elections, they become less interested in casting their vote due to the perception of lack of incentive (Bratton, 2008).
A study on the Nigerian election shows that violence reduces voter turnout and reduces competition for the candidates.
That survey shows that 71% said that the competition between political parties leads to violent clashes (Bratton, 2008).
The party with lower initial political support will resort to more political violence to reduce the competition.
The conflictual party activists use violence to force the competing party's ideological party supporters to vote in their favor or restrain them from voting by using violence.
In central Sri Lanka villages, people think electoral violence undermines the people's trust in politics and political parties.
It is one of the causes of electoral violence, and the political activists are targeted.
This means to people that involvement in politics has substantial dangers.
And this is why people abstain from participating in the election and evidently decrease the election's competitiveness (Höglund, 2009).
In the Philippines, the church and military have opposed the return of elitist democracy and worked for safe elections.
However, it has failed to eradicate poll violence because of the weak state, social disorder, and confrontational politics along with competitiveness (Linantud, 1998).
Control over resources: People compete in the elections to control the state because it is the only way to control the state resources.
This is why incumbents want to stay in power, and the opposition wants to come to power through an election.
And when there is a chance or any means they can use to come to power, they are not afraid to use it even if it is killing people.
This section has been divided into four subheadings: control over the state, power sharing, regional interests, and available resources.

Control over the state: Many political parties, also incumbents, use their followers to participate in the violence to win elections to control the state, and if they can control the state, they have access to resources.
In Nigeria, the state has a history of featuring violence in competition over who will have access to state resources (Angerbrandt, 2018).

On the other hand, in Ghana, the political party in government recruits party foot soldiers for committing electoral fraud and low-intensity electoral violence to win the election or maintain their control over state resources (Bob-Milliar, 2014).
In north and South Sudan, the government and rebel control compete and fight to control strategic towns and locations.
There are significant oil and economic resources, and to control these, there was a struggle between the main political contenders ahead of elections scheduled for 2015 (Höglund, 2009).
In the Philippines' 2007 election, different armed groups fighting for independent states participated in violent activities through pinprick ambushes and harassment tactics.
In addition, they operate in rural areas throughout the country and extort considerable sums of money from businesses and private citizens (Crost et al., 2013).
In most African countries, the political candidates, whether challenger or incumbent, resort to violence in the electoral contest to stay in power or gain power.
The incumbents in countries like Azerbaijan, Cambodia, Iran, or Zimbabwe have used violence in the election to stay in power.
And without an election, the gross violence in those countries would be fewer.
In Indonesia, the aspiring candidates target candidates and government agencies.

By targeting candidates, the aspirant candidates, literally reduce the number of competitors and increase their likelihood of winning and by targeting government agencies who are perceived to be responsible for holding elections and they push them for electronically beneficial decisions so that the aspirants can get to power and control state resources (Harish and Toha, 2017).
If the state feature is patrimonialism, the politicians gain power through informal networks, which they control through patronage.
And to run and form these informal networks, politicians use state resources (Höglund, 2009).
In Bangladesh, the incumbent pick up for power because there is a lack of a level playing field.
And the incumbent's desire and intention to remain in power encourage political and electoral violence.
By staying in power, the incumbent builds up a local power base using resources of local government institutions (Hossain and Rawnak, 2018).
By nature, elections are at a high stake, and it is a contest over state power, so conflict is inevitable.
It is linked with competition over political power by political parties and elites.
In Serbia, some incidents of violence during an election are state-motivated.
This is a part of the incumbent elites' power protection policy to maintain the state power's stronghold (Mochtak, 2016).
In Russia, electoral violence is used to prolong authoritarian rule.
To do so, the state uses an advanced coercion strategy (covering physical and psychological dimensions).
In Nigeria, the principal actors of organized violence during elections are mainly nonstate armed groups or political parties (who may also use the police and military).
The nonstate armed groups, particularly rebel groups, participate in the attack during election periods in pursuit of their political objectives, which is going to power.
International election observers can deter the government from postelection violence, but the opposition groups can easily deny the responsibility of violence.
To stay in power and avoid international pressure to participate in the electoral malpractice, the government increases repression over the opposition.
In the context of strong clientelism, the pre- and postvote violence is robustly associated with whether the incumbent is seeking reelection.

Those whose access to resources depends on the incumbent person will resort to violence, often through the state's security forces or ruling party's militia, to guarantee privileged access to power and patronage (Mochtak, 2016).
In Ethiopia, taking up arms and “going to the bush” has been the traditional way of acquiring political power.
However, in southern Ethiopia, due to the widespread protest, the government had to conduct reelection.
In the election, the opposition showed that peaceful and democratic resistance through well-prepared and well-organized parties could challenge any government and win elections.
Leaders with strong patronage linkage enabled them to control the activities and make the parties' most important decisions.
And getting a party ticket, is a ticket to an election, in Kenya has contributed to electoral violence during party primaries (Wanyama and Elklit, 2018).

The political economy of state capture: Bekoe (2012) described that capturing the state's political economy is one of the major causes of electoral violence with elites resorting to violence in order to gain or retain political power.
Power sharing: Political leaders, governments, and nonstate actors often sign power-sharing deals, which are, however, sometimes a consequence of violence.
Power sharing in the name of democracy has the perverse effects of engendering violence.

Nevertheless, power-sharing broad-based governing coalitions are generally inclusive of all major ethnic groups or political alliances in a given country, but the involved parties employ various types of coercion—including election violence—to reach a power-sharing deal (Höglund, 2009; Bekoe, 2012).
Regional interests: Political parties win elections and take control of the power and state resources, and then serve their own regional interests.

For instance, in Nigeria, elections are not about contestation of ideas and public policies but among hostile ethnoregional blocs, especially struggles for power among elite factional groups perceived as representing regional interests (Ashindorbe, 2018).

Höglund (2009) argued that to understand the local dynamics of electoral violence, we need to understand the regional variations; in many African countries, for example, the elected candidate represents regional interests (Höglund, 2009).

Resources in general: Election is about obtaining using power to control and then distribute national or regional resources to its formal and informal networks whom they have used to engage in electoral violence.

In Ghana, state-owned enterprises rewarded the party or regime supporters, and party foot soldiers expect monetary gifts as well as access to elected politicians in return for assisting their election to the office.

In addition, the winner-take-all system makes no room for opposition parties (except in the parliament) to participate in the government, which contributes to electoral violence in Ghana (Bob-Milliar, 2014).
Similarly, vote buying is possible for the incumbents because they have natural resources to spend on the electorate in general and on clienteles.
Incumbents can use resources controlled from office holding to influence the election, which is not an option for challengers.

In Kenyan elections, violence erupted because there was a perception of rigging elections, with more numerous incidents in areas with land-related conflicts and politically connected gangs, and rent-seeking behavior contributes to violence (Dercon and Gutiérrez-Romero, 2012).
In Kenya, where there is more population, there is more postelection violence.
In Zimbabwe, the percentage of the popular vote for opposition candidates impacts the number of postelection violence incidents (Hickman, 2011).

In some countries, a patron–client relationship is crucial, in which the patron provides protection, services, or rewards to the clients who becomes the patron's political supporter, and the politicians gain power through informal networks they control through the patronage of resources.
These clients help the politicians win elections with a promise of access to resources (Höglund, 2009).

Whoever holds political power controls the most economic assets of the state, so the incumbent also monopolizes the security forces and the legal means of violence in the state, facilitating their resorting to violence to win the election.
Election violence is sometimes a form of resistance against the authoritarian regime, however.
If the elections' results are close, tensions might escalate to electoral violence (Mochtak, 2016).

In a country like Nigeria, the power is very much concentrated in the center, which explains the mad rush to electoral power because those who win gain authority over the nation's natural and material resources.

In Russia, the natural resource–rich regions are more likely to experience manipulated elections, so that the winning candidate control natural resources (Moser and White, 2016), and Reeder and Seeberg (2018) find a similar high risk of electoral violence during candidate selections and final elections in Sub-Saharan African countries; stakes are even higher in presidential elections.

This access to resources affects the incumbent's likelihood of resorting to violence, often through the state's security forces or ruling party's militia, to guarantee privileged access to power and patronage.

In southern Ethiopia, the government tried to curtail and control the election, but the opposition was able to mobilize the people in a popular protest to challenge the government party's political hegemony, finally winning.
The incumbent monopolized the power and conducted elections at different times, but the opposition boycotted the election due to authoritarian and undemocratic practices.
The local administrative structure of governance and with this the incumbent control the peasantry (Höglund, 2009).
Personalism-patron client: Personalism has an impact on policy outcomes, with the fate of patrons depending on personal votes.
Patrons promise to deliver clientelist benefits to the voters, so that clients expect long-term benefits from enduring patron–client relationships (Hartlyn, 1994).
In Indonesia, where the state plays a dominant role in the economy, voters and candidates tend to form these patron–client relationships, resulting in high-level preference voting.
In political competition, personalism leads to interparty competition during elections (Bratton, 2008; Höglund, 2009).
History: To understand the causes of electoral violence of a particular region or a country, it is crucial to consider its electoral history and violence history.
A number of studies describe how the history of electoral misconduct and history of violent relations to control politics and state impact current electoral violence.
History of electoral misconduct: The democratic countries with a history of clean elections are less likely to experience electoral fraud or violence.

Elsewhere, electoral violence is adopted by political actors seeking to maximize their tenure in the office (Ruiz-Rufino, 2018), as in the Kaduna state of Nigeria with its history of violent local relations and subsequent violence after an election in that area escalated by local social networks (Angerbrandt, 2018).

History of violent relations to control politics and state: When the country has a history of damaging relations to influence politics and the state, the election might include violence as happened in Nigeria in a 2007 election that was accompanied by severe electoral violence.

The running president was unsuccessful in changing the constitution to allow him a third term; he tried to secure his brother's presidency, the state's military head, and apparently wanted to declare a state of emergency by provoking violence to prolong his rule (Bratton, 2008; Angerbrandt, 2018).
Elections are used to silence guns but can also provoke bullets.
The history of many democratic states provides evidence for this double link.
Elections attracted the medieval communities enormously, but their early history was troubled.

Political elites often mobilize voters around preexisting political and economic grievances by highlighting tensions and divisions among the communities, which US President Donald Trump did in his election campaigns.
Although it helped him get elected in 2016, the strategy backfired in 2020 mobilizing minority voters and those tired of his divisive rhetoric.

Those same divisions also precipitated unprecedented postelection violence with an armed assault on the US Capitol by Trump supporters protesting the election's validity and a deeply divided political culture.
Preexisting conflicts or ongoing civil wars increase the risk of election-related violence in many nations.

Institutions: In general, when the institutions that administer the elections lack credibility, the losers question the elections' results and undermine the entire democratic process; some critics can instigate electoral violence and sabotage the whole process (Fjelde and Höglund 2016).

Electoral violence can be seen as precipitated by five categories of institutional causes: (1) electoral rules; (2) electoral system institutions; (3) democratic institutions and their norms and values; (4) the type of governmental institutions; and (5) the very structure of relevant political and powerful institutions in a state.
Electoral rule: Rules of the game are fundamental to election violence.
Many studies on electoral violence have suggested that uneven or changing electoral rules can lead to significant electoral violence.
Stable institutions that are trusted and well-regarded are needed to sustain democracy.
In the 2007 Kenya election, one of the significant triggers of electoral violence was widespread “ignoring the law” (Dercon and Gutiérrez-Romero, 2012).
Elections can be a mechanism for aggregating preferences of a particular kind.

In a procedure recognized by an organization's rules—be it a state, club, voluntary organization, or whatever—all or some members choose a selected group to hold the organization's office and authority.
Elections rules that make the process free and fair are critical (Ruiz-Rufino, 2018).
Any violence contradicting an organization's laws to sabotage an election is considered electoral violence.
Formal rules in much of Africa, for example, are placed by majoritarian institutions that interact with powerful informal institutions such as patron–client relationships.
This ties political office to economic benefits for individual politicians, their families, and ethnic kinship networks.
The majoritarian rules tend to reward larger political parties disproportionately and impose higher barriers to political participation.

Under these rules, the perceived cost of defeat and permanent ban under majoritarian rules encourages both wings of the incumbency divide to use violence to influence the elections' outcome (Fjelde and Höglund, 2016).
One of the many ways to manage electoral violence is by clarifying the game rules and setting standards.
Electoral security can be ensured if the electoral institutions can create a situation where an election is not perceived as a zero-sum game and most parties and voters accept the game rules.
Legal reforms can improve the political system and state institutions' legitimacy.

In Serbia, many types of electoral violence (verbal attacks, intimidation, vandalism, property damage, and physical attacks with injuries or even death) were recorded in eight parliamentary, one federal presidential, and eight national presidential elections.
Many incidents were even state-motivated to maintain the incumbent elites' stronghold (Mochtak, 2016).
The Bangladesh government has also disregarded the rules and regulations of the election process leading to negative impacts on elections.
In the absence of effective rules and regulations, parties and candidates do whatever they want to do in the election (Momen, 2014).

In Kenya, many local and external organizations worked to improve the electoral system, creating an enhanced and more independent electoral commission, electoral rolls, vote tallying, and monitoring procedures, and addressing other issues surrounding the electoral process.
These are not self-enforcing, however, so they had to change rules arbitrarily and resort to extra-institutional and violent behavior.

In Nigeria, a retired army general and the president flagrantly and habitually disobeyed rulings from the courts on several occasions to control the party, including the candidature from the presidential level to local elections.
The president had no respect for the legislature, which he viewed as a subordinate to the executive.
In addition, he unleashed terror at will upon disloyal governors and politicians that stood in his path.
This is how incumbents use violence by ignoring the rules to win elections.
Electoral rules and electoral competition are the key determinants of electoral misconduct.

When incumbents perceive that the electoral competition will be tight and the electoral rules are majoritarian, the incumbents might lose; but to remain in power, they often use electoral misconduct (Ruiz-Rufino, 2018).

In Kenya and Ethiopia, electoral contests work as an epicenter of political violence because their security forces lack the basic ability to ensure law and order in a critical and challenging situation like an election (Smith, 2009).
Electoral system institutions: Electoral systems design and electoral institutions are the two significant parts of the whole process.

The electoral system shapes the incentive to engage in electoral misconduct; electoral designs can create or enhance opportunities through incentives and rewards for violations of electoral integrity and political manipulation.
Due to the lack of systemic design of the system, the voters suspect the voting process and portray it as a serious problem, leading to electoral violence.
In a Dominican Republic election campaign, electoral violence was marred due to the new voting system's orientation and the computerized system to count votes.
Many political parties urged going back to the old system.
In addition to the lack of budget and the way its judges are appointed, the Central Election Board of the Dominican Republic is weak and suffers from a lack of legitimacy (Hartlyn, 1994).
An electoral system must regulate the electoral process and police-military in managing and regulating violence during the electoral process.
Other institutions that directly affect the conflict dynamics are responsible for upholding security and enforcing the laws governing elections' conduct.
Electoral laws that regulate the mandate and power of the electoral commission, these candidature may create an impact on electoral violence (Höglund, 2009).

The electoral system that dampens voter turnout may encourage electoral fraud and in authoritarian regimes incumbents manipulate the electoral law for partisan achievements, hinder voter registration, prevent opposition parties from observing votes and the tally of the vote to reduce turnout.
In a proportional system, voter turnout is higher, and the voter turnout in a majoritarian system is lower (Moser and White, 2016).
In Gabon, elections are tainted by massive fraud, but the incumbent promises to establish an independent election commission, so the incumbent selectively coopts the government system's opposition.
In Bangladesh, the election commission is limited and believed to be partisan, so the oppositions have low and no trust in the process or the election outcome and there is electoral violence.

Momen (2014) claims that the regulatory framework and its enforcement are under the electoral system's challenge due to the lack of effective regulation although voters in this country expected a credible election system different from that previously instituted under military or semi-military regimes (Momen, 2014).
In a scenario where power is highly centralized and personalized, designed to skirt the law, and undermine the institutions' integrity, electoral violence is inevitable.
In the Malawian state, electoral institutions are funded by external funding.
This is why political leaders refrain from electoral violence due to the fear of canceling funding for those institutions and international legitimacy.
Institutions governing the electoral process are the essential ingredients to electoral violence (Höglund, 2009).
Political and electoral institutions that regulate electoral competition are the strong predictors of electoral misconduct in emerging democracies.
And majoritarian institutions like disproportional electoral systems are more likely to trigger electoral violence (Ruiz-Rufino, 2018).
And if the electoral system is designed only to benefit the winner, competitors will die to win the elections.

Election management capacity: In developing countries where political elites are not well defined, there is always a chance of electoral violence which is why the institutions involved in election management are essential to control the violence that might erupt.
As Bekoe (2012) pointed out, “election management capacity” of the electoral institutions is a significant contributor to electoral violence (Bekoe, 2012).

In some countries, elections are considered a means of conflict management, and to encounter political and social conflicts, international communities promote free and fair elections in those conflict-prone areas.
If the authorities responsible for managing those elections are not capable enough and trustworthy, then electoral violence is virtually inevitable (Salehyan and Linebarger, 2015).
Single-member districts: A single-member district (SMD) under a plurality or majority system is an electoral district that returns one officeholder to a body with multiple legislative members.
In SMD, candidates gain more from electoral manipulation than in the proportional representation (PR) system.
In addition, to alter the election's outcome, the SMD candidate requires fewer voters than in the PR system.
With manipulation, electoral violence is one way to influence the election outcome.
Some argue that PR is associated with more electoral violence than the SMD because SMD leaders can later be held accountable for the violence during the election (Ruiz-Rufino, 2018).
Failure of democratic institutions: The failure of democratic institutions and their norms, values, ideas can bring and provoke violence in an election.
In South Africa, the democratic system failed to address poverty, inequality, and racial discrimination by undermining the justice system, severely limiting people's participation.
It opened up a space for internal aggression and conflict and reflected in that country's election.
In Côte d’Ivoire, principled exclusion in the name of democracy has led to violence.
To exacerbate and mitigate violence, democratic institutional design and reform are crucial (Bekoe, 2012).
Election violence is a threat to democracy.
The more they try to overcome this threat in Nigeria, the more hydra-headed electoral violence it grows.

Due to the lack of institutions in a democratic system prosecuting the election, violent offenders make electoral violence an insignificant offense, giving offenders impunity and encouraging their future participating in this offense.

Elections are held under a predefined electoral system in a democratic institution, which should include a deliberate attempt to reorient and reeducate the citizens about the meanings and implications of democratic elections.

In the Dominican Republic, the election in 1994 was flawed and prone to crisis because of the political regime's fragility and the low legitimacy of the state's democratic institutions and the basic political processes.
The country's weak electoral institutions and the political parties' attitude and behavior led to the destruction of democratic institutions and sparked electoral violence (Hartlyn, 1994).
In Ukraine, the business sector was integrated into political life.
But due to the postcommunist world's economic condition, the state had weak institutions and rule of law.

The bosses—economically and politically influential actors—took advantage of those limitations to build their economic empire and patronage network extended to political activities eventually leading to electoral corruption (Herron and Sjoberg, 2016).

Linantud (1998) argued that terrorism and fraud intruded on the Philippines' election and democracy remained incomplete weaking the Filipino state and causing violence in its elections (Linantud, 1998).
In Sub-Saharan Africa, most electoral violence is committed by incumbents seeking reelection.
A country's quality of democracy impacts the failure of democratic institutions (Mochtak, 2016).
Preexisting social conflicts, poor-quality founding elections, weak economic growth, and an instability of democratic institutions shape electoral violence.
Bangladesh's politics and governance are trying to exercise a one-party government instead of a real parliamentary democracy, and none of the elections so far was free and fair.
This led to the fragile condition of democracy in which elections have failed to meet international standards of electoral integrity, voter turnout, and electoral malpractice.
The Election Commission of Bangladesh has been unable to ensure a level playing field for the political parties to compete (Momen, 2014).

Kenyan political elites and the successive regimes have failed to bring the desired change of the democratic institution and constitution and framed the election as a process for political elites' time-bound power contests.
Ethiopia has had extensive and substantive constitutional reforms, but no negotiated pacts among the political elites.

Consequently, any open and competitive campaign period and a well-attended election would be followed by violence and a security crackdown by the incumbents due to the lack of democratic polity (Smith, 2009).
Government system: Many studies found that a particular country's government system is an instigator of electoral violence.

After the 2017 election, winner parties formed a coalition government in Kenya, putting election corruption at the front of the opposition's demand for electoral justice (Dercon and Gutiérrez-Romero, 2012).
The president was more interested in the crackdown on opposition parties, leading to a demand for a return to the parliamentary form of government.
Elections are being advocated by the international community as a peacebuilding strategy.
Citizens can thereby establish a legitimate and representative democratic government, and hope eventually to end ongoing conflicts (Höglund, 2009).
In a government's presidential form, to select the president and parliamentary system of the dominant government party chooses the prime minister.
Whatever the form of government, an undemocratic system will spark violence as they encourage parties to mobilize but with little voice (Salehyan and Linebarger, 2015).

Structural and institutional: According to many social scientists, “structure” itself is responsible for violence, especially when it comes to electoral violence, in which many different structures and institutions are involved including the political, power, and incentive structures as organizational and competitiveness structures related to elections.
Bekoe (2012) claims that structures and institutions are the drivers of election violence in many developing countries (Bekoe, 2012).
In the Dominican Republic, the immediate cause of flawed elections is the political, social structure related to presidentialism and its electoral institutions.
The socioeconomic structure and high employment, weak civil society, and high poverty level have also contributed to the country's election-related violence (Hartlyn, 1994).
Outside of consolidated democracies, the electoral structure of leader selection influences the violence in the election.
When incumbents are restricted from using election rigging strategies, the electoral structure allows them to allocate power and hold the leaders accountable peacefully.
If the restrictions are compromised, however, violence in the election is inevitable.
A study on electoral violence in Bangladesh showed how the incumbents use the political and constitutional institutions to ensure their tenure in power.
International pressure: Most of the developing democracies in the world face international pressure of some sort.
In case of elections, the international community sends election observers.
Based on their reports, the international community tries to assess the election's credibility and integrity.

The participation of the international electoral observers sometimes shifts the election-day violence to preelection violence, however, because on election day, local and international observers with intensive media support can expose election-day violence internationally and the incumbents will lose their legitimacy.
Many international observers were criticized for placing too much emphasis on election-day violence and ignoring pre- and postelection violence (Daxecker, 2012).

Legitimacy: When international election observers indicate that fraud has occurred, and reports published by monitoring organizations have drawn attention from the international communities, it harms the legitimacy of a regime and bolsters the case of aggrieved groups.
Sometimes, to gain legitimacy and acceptance from the international community, incumbents will cancel an election and declare new elections (Daxecker, 2012).
Mandates of observers: In some cases, mandates are unclear about what electoral observers want.
When their observation and methodology of observation are elusive and their reports hesitant, incumbents can easily bend and use them in their favor.
Manipulated reports can instigate violence even before they can be checked.

International observers can play a vibrant role in reducing violence by mediating among domestic actors; they can deter violence, detect manipulation, or simply just observe and certify a free and fair election.

Election observation is a standard policy for promoting good governance and democratic institutions in formally autocratic countries or countries where there is a lack of democratic polity (Daxecker, 2012).
In Kenya, after 2007, election violence erupted, and the election commission was blamed for manipulating the election result, international observers supported the claim.
Elections are supposed to remove bad leaders from power and resolve the social conflict mutually; observers are there to ensure the process has no impediment.
The presence of the electoral observer may paradoxically increase the chance of electoral violence, however.
Participants have an incentive to play to an international audience when electoral observers are present (Salehyan and Linebarger, 2015).
Electoral observers can deter violence in the incumbents' election; however, the opposition groups sometimes use violence in the elections expecting criticism from the international observer groups.
In the end, they can easily deny responsibility and successfully blame the government for the violence.

Another study suggests little support for the presence of international election observers as a cause of electoral violence, but when they draw attention to electoral fraud after the election, the probability of postelection violence is relatively higher.
Socioeconomic characteristics: Many studies have argued that a particular country's socioeconomic characteristics have a big impact on electoral violence.
Especially in developing economies and that have fewer socioeconomic opportunities, election violence is common.
Besides, the people in those regions have less confidence in voting technologies.
Demographics: Some studies claim that the demographics (age, education, income, background, and place of residence) of the area have an impact on electoral violence.

A study in Pakistan has tried to show that youth or younger generations, especially the youths studying in universities or colleges, had more favorable perceptions about election violence and electoral malpractice.
In addition, the socioeconomic inequality of the people makes the elections endangered to election violence.
Likewise, the perception of electoral integrity and electoral rigging is linked, and to change it, the policymakers have to come forward.
In Nigeria, there is a clear correlation between demographics and electoral malpractice.
In both the 2003 and 2007 elections in Nigeria, the poor people were approached by a politician or their agent have offered to buy their vote.
In addition, older people are more significantly more likely to vote than the younger generation, and women are very much less likely to vote than men.
Above all, education has a significance on voting choices (Bratton, 2008).
In Serbia, socioeconomic conflict persists as a matter of inequality of income.

Socioeconomic conflict works as an escalation factor for electoral violence if the income inequality is high enough to motivate the economically deprived population to engage in violent strategy (Mochtak, 2016).
In Africa, social conflicts are associated with electoral violence, and so does in Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, India, and Thailand.
The study by Salehyan and Linebarger (2015) argued that most African elections encounter electoral violence, especially the developing countries.

Election violence is widespread in the poorest countries because they do not have enough capacity to effectively and efficiently carry out the elections and administer them (Salehyan and Linebarger, 2015).
From a violent perspective, the more impoverished society with lower income and education provides an easy way to recruit participants for violence.
In this case, the cost of electoral violence will be lower, and the incumbents and the challengers will be more interested in using violence to win elections.
On the other hand, some locations have shown that higher levels of schooling or educational attainment increase public consciousness of electoral misconduct during local elections.
Usually, the case is in poorer countries recruiting thugs is easier, and the institutions are weaker, so election violence is easy before or after the election.
Trust on voting technologies: The developing, democratic institutions are less efficient, and influential people have less confidence in voting technologies.
In the United States, the voters are interested in electronic voting technologies on the other hand, and they are also concerned about electoral fraud and ballot security.
A study shows that a small number of voters are concerned about electronic voting technology–related fraud.
On the other hand, they are more concerned about potential forms of election fraud, such as registering ineligible voters or voter suppression in the United States.
On the other hand, political polarization increases the older respondents' concern about fraud when used in electoral voting.
In India, electronic voting machines (EVMs) has significantly decreased electoral fraud.
EVM also made the electoral process more competitive for the candidates who participate in the election.
It also declined the winning margins and the vote share of the winning candidates.
EVM may have helped declining electoral fraud but has increased the competitiveness, which might trigger electoral violence.

Violence in the election is usually instigated by the political actors, incumbents, and oppositions to deter voters from voting; however, the major bulk of violence breaks loose when the election results are published, and there are hotspots of the contending parties (Dercon and Gutiérrez-Romero, 2012).
One large subgroup in this area is the use of the Internet by political interest groups and as a tool for political parties.
Throughout the 1990s, the Internet became an extremely politicized tool for elections, campaigns, and policy agenda formation.
By the beginning of the 21st century most candidates and political parties in countries where elections are considered democratic had regularly updated Web sites.
In addition, there were countless interest groups, think tanks, and grass roots organizations that posted their positions.
There were also media Web sites that gathered and analyzed election-related information in unprecedented scope and depth.
Finally, there was the explosion of parody sites, Web pages that made fun of candidates and positions, some overtly and others subtly.
Though the complete, often complex effects of the Internet are just beginning to be systematically studied, there is anecdotal evidence of the impact the Internet has had on democratic processes.
For example, some scholars credit the Internet for the gubernatorial victory of 3rd party candidate Jesse Ventura in the state of Minnesota.

Virtually a neglected candidate for much of the race, there is evidence that Ventura's Web sites, coupled with his name recognition as a professional wrestler, were instrumental in mobilizing general support and eventually votes.
One area that has been more of an issue in the United States, but is also becoming one in some other democratic countries, is the mobilization of the electorate to actually get out and cast votes.
A related subject is that experiments with voting over the Internet have been somewhat successful and the possibilities for widespread use of this technique are on the horizon.
But, the Internet has also been used as a forum for voter motivation.
In the United States, for example, the nonprofit “Rock the Vote” campaign is designed to inspire a younger generation to be more involved in politics.
Part of its success is its partnership with the global media organization MTV.
Even between elections, the movement has made an attempt via its Web site and other media to keep youth politically engaged.
Ads and any other forms of communication regarding products, services, or business.
A federal law governing maximum levels of campaign contributions with requirements of public reporting of campaign donations and expenditures.
A federal law that placed further restrictions on campaign contributions and restricted the activities of nonaffiliated PACs.
A federal agency charged with enforcing FECA and location for filing of required campaign financial information.
Approvision in the U.S. Constitution that guarantees an individual the right to speak without censorship of content (with only limited exceptions).

A formally created group of citizens, trade associations, businesses, or employees organized for the purpose of raising funds or making campaign expenditures to or on behalf of candidates or ballot propositions.
Ads and any other forms of communication regarding candidates or ballot initiatives.
A set of voluntary guidelines passed by the U.S. Senate on campaign spending limits, PACs, independent expenditures, and soft money.

Named for the section of the Internal Revenue Code that gives them tax-exempt status, these are nonprofit organizations that engage in voter registration and education programs, which can raise unlimited funds and engage in unlimited independent expenditures.

Named for the section of the Internal Revenue Code that gives them tax-exempt status, there are 501(c) (3) organizations such as church and charitable organizations that are not permitted to engage in political activities and 501(c) (4) organizations that are known as social welfare organizations and that can engage in political activities that are not their primary purpose.
